blurb: Radar, EO/IR, SIGINT, sonar, hyperspectral and quantum sensing, plus GNSS, inertial, terrain and celestial navigation and missile seekers — compared on range, counter-stealth, jam resistance, and cost.
question: How does this system find a target and know where it is?
title: Sensing and Navigation: A Practical Reference
lede: Finding something and knowing where you are turn out to be the same problem solved from opposite ends, and both get harder the moment someone jams you. This guide covers {{N_ENTRIES}} sensing and navigation technologies across seven classes, with detection range, performance against low-observable targets, jam resistance, and cost.

facets.label: Function
facets.tip: What the system is for: Search (wide-area detection), Track (maintain a track good enough for fire control), Identify (classify or fingerprint what was found), Navigate (know where you are), Terminal (guide a weapon in the last phase).

facets.label: Range
facets.tip: Useful detection or acquisition envelope against a typical target. Near (<1 km) · Short (1–20 km) · Medium (20–200 km) · Long (200–1,000 km) · Strategic (1,000 km+). Navigation sensors that measure the platform rather than the world carry no range tag.

facets.label: Vs stealth
facets.tip: How well the sensor performs against a low-observable target. Shaping and radar-absorbent material are tuned against centimetric fire-control radar, so long-wavelength, multistatic, and passive infrared approaches all do relatively better. Navigation systems carry no tag here.

facets.label: Jam resist
facets.tip: Resistance to deliberate interference — jamming, spoofing, decoys, or obscurants. Poor = defeated by widely available equipment · Fair = degraded by a capable opponent · Good = needs a specific, expensive counter · Strong = no practical remote attack, usually because the system emits nothing.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional unit cost of one installed system at typical production quantities, not the program that developed it. A seeker on a missile and a shipborne radar differ by four orders of magnitude, which is most of why the sheet spans this range.
